title: DNS: finding an IP address, step by step
intro: Computers need numbers, not names. Follow the chain of servers that turns www.example.com into an IP address.

predict.question: The resolver asks a ROOT server for www.example.com. What does the root answer?
options: The address of the .com TLD servers
predict.reveal: Root servers only know who runs each top-level domain. It points to the .com servers, which point onward to example.com's own server.

takeaway: DNS is a chain of referrals: root, TLD, authoritative. The resolver follows it once and caches the answer for next time.

steps.say: Your browser needs the IP of www.example.com. It asks the resolver, a helper run by your ISP. Cache is empty, so the resolver does the legwork.
First stop: a root server. Every resolver knows the root addresses by heart.
The root does not know the IP. It only knows who runs each ending, and sends the resolver to the .com servers.
Second stop: the .com TLD (top-level domain) servers.
The TLD server knows every .com domain and who looks after each. It points to example.com's own name server.
Third stop: the authoritative server, the one that owns the records for example.com.
At last a real answer: the IP address, plus a TTL (time to live) saying how long it may be remembered.
The resolver hands the IP to your browser and keeps a copy in its cache for 300 seconds. The browser can now connect.
A moment later someone asks for www.example.com again. The resolver answers from cache: no root, TLD or authoritative trips.
After the TTL runs out the entry is dropped and the chain starts again, so changed IPs spread. Referrals once, cache after.
